outcomes: A TypeScript project builds, type-checks, tests, lints, serves and packages without a per-project bundler, runner or formatter configuration
Building many projects in one invocation produces exactly what building each of them alone produces, and one project's failure does not change another project's output
A workspace pins one version per shared dependency, and a freshly scaffolded project installs against that pin without editing the workspace root by hand
An npm tarball or Docker image loads under the same loader rules the workspace used, so a packaged project does not fail at import time in a consumer's runtime
A Node service declares the Node runtime and runs on Node from serve to its container image, while Bun keeps building it
A library whose build script runs tsc alone keeps that tsc and gains Putnami's cache: its output lands and is restored where the packages that depend on it resolve its main and exports
nonGoals: Replacing Bun as the task runtime, linting with a tool other than Biome or ESLint, formatting with a tool other than Biome, or exposing the configuration surface of Bun, Biome, ESLint, Vitest or Jest as Putnami configuration: a project chooses its test runner and its linter, which keep reading their own configuration files, a library whose build script runs tsc alone keeps that tsc, which Bun runs, and the installer is the package manager the repository declares, never a Putnami option
Owning application framework behaviour — routing, rendering, persistence and DI belong to the @putnami/* packages this extension builds
Publishing to a registry: package prepares the tarball or image and records channels, publish uploads them
Promising compatibility across every pre-1.0 minor release, which RELEASE.md governs

requirements.text: Build runs as independently cached phases — generate, transpile and types or tsc, plus compile — and each project in a batched phase writes only into its own output directory, including the type-checker's incremental build-info state. A tsc phase writes only the outputs its project's tsconfig names, never a referenced project's.
A batched phase produces the same per-project artifacts as running that phase for one project alone.

When one project in a batch fails, the failure is attributed to that project and the sibling projects' outputs are still produced; a generate failure always emits a diagnostic rather than an empty non-zero result.
A project's build content hash is a deterministic function of its inputs, so an unchanged project produces an unchanged identity.

With Bun or pnpm, workspace install seeds a missing catalog entry for every @putnami/* dependency a member references through the catalog: protocol, in the root package.json for Bun and pnpm-workspace.yaml for pnpm, in the named catalog when one was requested, keeping existing entries, the manifest's key order and the file's other lines. The seed is the latest dist-tag, with no request, unless the putnami-channel job option names a channel: then its exact version, or a failure. npm and yarn get none.

Serve resolves its entrypoint from the project's "./serve" export unless one is passed explicitly, and reports a user-facing error when no package manifest or no such export exists instead of guessing a file.

A served or run child process forwards its own exit code; an interrupt terminates the whole child process group and reports 130, escalating to SIGKILL when the group does not exit within the grace period.

Transpiled library output does not depend on the builder's environment: JSX compiles to the production automatic runtime (react/jsx-runtime) whatever NODE_ENV or bunfig.toml the builder has, and process.env reads, NODE_ENV included, stay runtime reads for the consumer.
A staged npm package loads under the loader rules of the CLI contract it claims, and a stale lower claim is ratcheted to the earned one.

A build graph built with the node target fails with typescript.bun_api_on_node when a module it reaches, its dependencies included, references the Bun global or imports bun or a bun: module outside a typeof Bun guard, and the diagnostic names each such module and the import chain from the entrypoint that reaches it. The build documentation lists the @putnami/* packages whose server exports load on Node, and that list is the one the same check computes.

An npm package whose extension manifest declares agent content carries the tree built from its authored source under the package's name and version, bound by the digest the packaged manifest declares and stamped with the agent-content contract; a manifest without agent content keeps the base contract. A files allowlist that would drop the content, content the policy forbids, and a content path the package already holds fail packaging.

Packaging records the channel it produced inside the output directory it owns, never at the package root; the index is derived over every owned record, sibling packagers record independently, and a channel is never recorded twice.
A project that declares public assets fails packaging loudly when those assets are absent, rather than producing an image that 404s at runtime.

The lint command and its tasks cover every project file Biome can rewrite and never read or rewrite a file under a nested project root (a subdirectory with its own putnami.json, outside a symbolic link and the directories the cache key skips), resolve the workspace configuration from the config root while keeping an external configuration anchored at the project root, and bind the scheduler's CPU budget without overriding an explicit thread setting.

A project's linter is options["@putnami/typescript"].lint.linter, biome or eslint, else eslint when its package.json lint script runs eslint, else Biome; a configuration file present never chooses, and another value fails lint with typescript.lint_linter_unknown. An ESLint project runs no Biome formatter, and a batch lints each project with its own linter, its ESLint members in parallel.

ESLint lint runs the nearest node_modules/.bin/eslint, from the project up to the workspace, with the Node on PATH, over . from the project directory, outside nested projects; the lint script's arguments are not run, and lint warns naming them. Each message becomes a diagnostic with file, line, column and rule; --fix applies fixes, --fix false only reports. Configuration and ignore files and the file types ESLint plugins lint are cache inputs. A missing eslint or node fails naming it.

Build, the serve of a project on the Bun runtime, a test run by Bun and a lint run by Biome need Bun and no node program on the host. Lint starts the native Biome executable of the host's platform package, @biomejs/cli-<os>-<arch> or its -musl variant on a musl host, on every operating system and in a hoisted or an isolated install. Without that package, lint starts Biome's JavaScript launcher with the task's Bun, never with a node from PATH.

Workspace dependency installation materializes the extension's Biome rules as the workspace-root configuration when the workspace has none, preserves an existing one byte-for-byte, and fails explicitly when the extension default cannot be read or parsed. The Biome devDependency it adds is the exact release those rules' schema names. The rules keep every specs.baseline.json expanded, as `putnami specs baseline --update` writes it.

Workspace install of a workspace that installs with Bun declares the bun it installs with as the root package.json packageManager, bun@<version>, when that manifest exists and declares none, so the lock written after the installers pins the bun the task runtime probes. It keeps an existing declaration and the manifest's key order, creates no manifest, and declares no bun whose version is not a plain release.

The task runtime lists the Bun the CLI provisions under the Putnami home as a candidate, and a Bun install or fetch runs the bun the CLI resolved. With no bun on PATH, a job runs the release the lock pins, else the declared or default one, from toolchains/bun/bun-<version>. The extension installs no Bun: with none, a job fails naming that release and `putnami install`, and requests nothing. A Bun there, at bun-<target>/bun or bin/bun, keeps its caches in its folder's install/cache, never in ~/.bun.

The TypeScript extension answers `__putnami toolchain-resolve` with one bun pin: the release the root package.json declares as packageManager, else the extension's default release. A committed lock version 5 pin of that release is kept as committed. The default release is pinned offline from the digests the extension ships; another declared release is pinned from the SHA-256 digests its GitHub release lists, and offline it is a problem whose remedy is `putnami install` with network access.

Workspace install writes the complete membership in the job context, with the workspace-sync task's code, where the package manager reads it: packages of pnpm-workspace.yaml for pnpm, keeping its other lines, else workspaces of the root package.json. It writes before it seeds the catalog and installs, so a project created after the last projects sync is installed, leaves an unchanged list and a context without the membership untouched, and fails before installing when it cannot read or write the list.

Workspace install runs the package manager the root package.json names in packageManager, bun, npm, pnpm or yarn, else the one the root names by its files: bun.lock or bun.lockb, pnpm-lock.yaml or pnpm-workspace.yaml, yarn.lock, then package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json. With none it runs Bun. It runs npm, pnpm and yarn from PATH and fails naming the manager when PATH has none, fails on any other packageManager name, and writes no lockfile of another manager.

The extension's workspace inputs and install inputs name the lockfile of every package manager it installs with and pnpm-workspace.yaml, so a change to the lockfile in use invalidates the cache of the TypeScript tasks and makes the installed workspace stale.

putnami upgrade --deps pins the @putnami/* versions in the catalog the workspace declares, in the root package.json, else in pnpm-workspace.yaml, else in the root dependencies, then reinstalls with the workspace's package manager and its own reinstall flag. It writes no lockfile of another manager, and a failed install restores the root package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml and that manager's lockfiles.

Workspace install creates the root package.json when it is missing, before any other step reads it: a private package named after the workspace, the name in putnami.workspace.json else the root directory's name, with the members listed in workspaces unless pnpm-workspace.yaml lists them. It never touches an existing file, so a second install rewrites nothing. Projects sync still creates no root package.json.

On a hosted run, workspace-fetch reads the handed credential before it starts a process, then downloads what the committed lockfile names into the manager cache from a scratch copy, its bearer only in a private .npmrc or .yarnrc.yml it removes. No process it starts runs a script, a pnpmfile, a Yarn plugin or a yarnPath, and it refuses a manager inside the workspace and pnpm configDependencies. The install is then frozen and offline from that cache. Without that lockfile the fetch fails; no job rewrites it.
Build hooks contributed by dependencies are discovered and invoked in a deterministic order: ranked manifests first, remaining manifests in a stable order, and invocation follows discovery.

Hook discovery fails, before any hook runs, when a dependency the project declares is not installed in the node_modules of the project or of a directory above it up to the workspace root, so generate never succeeds without the hooks its dependencies contribute and never caches an incomplete .gen under the key of a complete one.

Each log event a pre-build or config-extract hook emits reaches the task's event stream, in order, at its level, with trace shown as debug, whether the hook succeeds or fails; in a batched generate, each log names the member project it belongs to.
putnami test --rerun-each N, under its flag or its rerunEach option, passes --rerun-each=N to bun test, so each test file of the project runs N times; without it each file runs once.

A project's test runner is the runner parameter of the test command (bun, vitest or jest), set by --runner or options["@putnami/typescript:test"].runner, else the runner its package.json test script runs, else Bun. Vitest and Jest run the bin entry of their package in the node_modules of the project or the workspace with the node on PATH; with no node the task fails and names node. A Vitest or Jest project's tests are type-checked with its own tsconfig's compiler options.

Every test runner writes results.junit.xml and lcov.info into the task's output: Vitest through its junit reporter and lcov coverage reporter, Jest through its --json result converted to JUnit, so no reporter package is required, and its lcov coverage reporter. The summary and --enforce-coverage read them as they read Bun's. The runner parameter, the runner's configuration and setup files and __tests__ directories are inputs of the task's cache key.

Test and coverage results are parsed into structured per-file and per-project reports, uncovered project sources are counted, external dependencies are excluded, and a missing report file is an empty result rather than a crash.

Test runs emit one deterministic structured outcome summary by default, retain the complete transcript as session-detail log events, bound causal failure diagnostics to the CLI report limits with explicit omission accounting, and let test-verbose change visibility without changing the Bun invocation, result data or verdicts.

The test command type-checks every TypeScript file of the project, tests, fixtures, benchmarks and dot-directories such as .gen included, with the project's tsconfig and the compiler options of the types phase, and emits nothing: a type error or an unused @ts-expect-error in any of them fails the command. The types phase still checks only src, bin and .gen. A dot-named file stays out, as in the types phase, and a file under node_modules, dist or a nested project root is left to its owner.
The runtime manifest a locally-prepared extension serves and the one a packaged archive ships describe the same runtime, so an installed extension behaves as the workspace one did.

The extension owns the npm ecosystem profile and uses the oci profile; a project yields an npm member only for declared package publication intent and an oci member only for declared image publication intent, with the exact package and publish steps recorded so malformed packaging is diagnosed instead of silently hiding a requested artifact. OCI coordinates retain the native repository namespace from the effective workspace or project registry entry, excluding only the host.
The workspace registries entry for npm drives the scope lines written to .npmrc and the publish registry; no registry URL is hard-coded.
Every npm publication, new or reused, reports one published member with its verified digest and writes no dist-tag.

A release-set npm publication that uploads itself sends the read that checks whether the version exists, the upload, and the read that verifies it again after a transient registry failure, a bounded number of times. It uploads again only after a read shows the registry does not serve the version.

When the engine names a publication outbox, a release-set npm member and a Docker image for the managed registry are packed into it with a descriptor that names their bytes, and the job resolves no credential, sends no registry request, writes nothing else outside its build outputs and reports no published member. Publication to any other registry ignores the outbox, and without one, publication is unchanged.

A dry-run npm publication asks the registry, without writing, whether it already holds the staged package at its version, and emits one member-probe event: absent, identical when the registry copy equals the tarball the real publish would upload, conflict when it differs or cannot be compared, unverified when the registry cannot answer. A release-set member sends one GET of the tarball, with a bearer only when one resolved, and runs no npm process. Any other publication asks through npm view and npm pack.

A dist-tag upgrade reads a packument of any realistic size. A package the registry answers as absent, or whose packument has no dist-tag for the channel, keeps its version and is named in a warning diagnostic. Any other lookup failure stops the upgrade before it writes anything.
The upgrade table shows, for every resolved version, the source revision carried by its suffix.

The generated TypeScript client build-generate emits into the project tree is committed, and build-generate is its first writer in a session; its declared client output carries drift: fail, so the engine compares what the task writes (or a cache hit restores) with the bytes present before and fails the task with generated-output-drift when they differ, leaving the regenerated client in the worktree to commit. Build-time generation under .gen carries no policy.

The OpenAPI contract build-generate writes to schema/openapi.json is committed, and build-generate is its first writer in a session; its declared openapi output carries drift: fail, so a committed contract that differs from the one openapi() regenerates fails the task with generated-output-drift, leaving the regenerated contract in the worktree to commit.

Once every preBuild hook reports data.httpRoutes {v:1,state:complete}, build-generate commits canonical HTTP routes atomically, skips identical bytes, commits routes [] for an empty fragment and removes the file with no fragment. An absent, malformed or unavailable evaluation, failed hook, invalid aggregate, unreadable manifest or missing Bun fails generate, naming the cause, and keeps committed routes and infra facts. Solo and batch commit identical bytes. Drift fails the task. No option controls it.

build-generate writes the project's TypeScript feature evidence under .gen, and the evidence names the project's source binding. Its cache policy declares sourceBound, so a cached generate serves only at the binding its evidence names: an edit outside its key, such as a test file, a spec or putnami.features.json, executes generate once at the new binding and moves neither its key nor any dependent key. Hook code and manifest edits move generate and dependent keys.

Validate holds the breaking-change marker for a TypeScript package the support catalog selects for a stable-only consumer: an entry point, an export or a member removed, a changed kind or reduced visibility since the last release of the project's line fails, naming the package and the symbol, unless a commit since that tag that touches the project declares it breaking. A change of written type warns and passes. Additions pass. A release the check cannot read warns.
The TypeScript extension's publish-docker task declares the docker channel and publish-npm the npm channel, and no other task declares one.
The npm packager refuses to publish an extension manifest without a name, a hook-only one included, before it stamps a contract, and leaves the staged manifest as staged.

A project declares the runtime of its workload as options["@putnami/typescript"].runtime in its putnami.json, bun or node, and runs on bun when it declares none; any other value fails the job with typescript.invalid_runtime, naming both values. On node, build transpiles with the node target unless the command names a target, and a project that compiles with tsc runs the node-target check after tsc.

On node, the compile step writes a Node bundle in place of a Bun executable: the compile entrypoint as an ES module with the project's own modules and its workspace dependencies bundled, its installed packages left as imports, and a linked source map.

On node, serve bundles the serve entrypoint, the ./serve export else the run entrypoint, as compile does, and starts node --enable-source-maps on it with the environment, port and log forwarding of a Bun serve. The bundle resolves packages from the project's node_modules. With watch on, it rebuilds when a file the bundle was built from changes and restarts node; a rebuild that fails reports its errors and keeps the running process and its bundle.

On node, run bundles the run entrypoint once and starts node --enable-source-maps on it, and putnami run exits with the program's exit code. With no node on PATH, serve and run fail with typescript.node_not_found, naming node.

On node, package --docker assembles the image from the Node bundle and the production dependencies the project's installed node_modules resolve: its dependencies and optionalDependencies and theirs, never a devDependency, under /app/node_modules. A dependency that is not installed fails the task, naming it and putnami install. The container starts node --enable-source-maps on the bundle.

The base of a Node image is the digest-pinned distroless Node image of the major the project declares: package.json engines.node, else .nvmrc or .node-version in the project, then at the workspace root. A project that declares none fails with typescript.node_version_undeclared, naming those three fields, and a major with no pinned base fails naming the majors that have one.

A project's compiler is the compiler parameter of build, test, serve, run and package, set by options["@putnami/typescript"].compiler or --compiler: bun, tsc or auto, the default. Under auto it is tsc when the package.json build script runs tsc alone (tsc, tsc -b or tsc -p with at most one config, plus --pretty or --verbose, and nothing else), else bun. A tsc project runs no Bun transpile or types step; an explicit tsc whose build script is something else fails naming it.

With tsc, build runs the compiler of the first node_modules/typescript from the project directory up to the workspace root with the task's Bun, never node, and never downloads one; a missing tsc fails naming typescript. It runs the build script's tsc command, except that tsc -b on a config with references runs as tsc -p, since Putnami builds or restores each reference first. With no build script it runs tsc -p on tsconfig.lib.json, else tsconfig.json.

With tsc, build declares the config's outDir, and its declarationDir and .tsbuildinfo where they lie outside the outDir, as its outputs. A run empties them before tsc starts, a cache hit restores them in place, and every job of a project that depends on it runs after it, as do the compile, serve and run jobs of the project. An outDir that is unset, outside the project, the project itself, not ignored by Git, or holding a file Git tracks fails the build before tsc runs, naming the setting.

The key of a tsc build reads every file of the project Git does not ignore, the JSON configuration files at the top of each project of its dependency closure and its tsconfig files, the root tsconfig files and lockfiles, and the key of each dependency's tsc build. test plans the same step for each project it tests, so a run that tests a library and its dependent runs the dependent's tests after the library's tsc and keys them on it.
The npm packager of package refuses a project that compiles with tsc, naming it, rather than packing a tarball without its compiled code.
